newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German parties jockey for lead in "Berlin Republic".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German parties jockey for lead in "Berlin Republic".

text.p: Germany doesn't face a general election for almost another two years, but its political parties are already starting to jockey for position as if the race were just about to begin.

At stake is the balance of power in the "Berlin Republic", the united Germany that evolves after the politicians turn their backs on sleepy Bonn after 50 years of back-room dealing there and move to pulsating Berlin in 1999.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) have made the most dramatic start for the 1998 campaign, luring into their ranks seven former east German civil rights campaigners who fear their left-wing friends might soon start working together with ex-communists.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) seem to be planning just that. A strategy paper that was to stay confidential but didn't proposes local and state-level links with the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successors to the hardline Marxists who ruled East Germany for 40 years.

"The cards are being reshuffled for an election to show the way into the future," commented the Leipziger Volkszeitung, the main newspaper in the eastern city that launched the protests that led to German reunification in 1990.
"The split in the ranks of the civil rights campaigners seven years after the Berlin Wall fell is a belated but quite normal sorting out of the political spectrum in Germany."
SMALL PARTIES ALSO PREPARING
Bonn's small parties have also been been laying the groundwork for 1998.

The pro-business Free Democrats (FDP) almost broke up their 14-year coalition with Kohl in recent months by insisting -- successfully -- on tax cuts that only make Finance Minister Theo Waigel's austerity drive more difficult.
And the once-radical Greens moved steadily towards the political centre, hoping to find enough votes there to be a junior coalition partner after the election due in late 1998.
The German political scene has been split since the country reunited, with a firm four-party system in the west but only three parties of note in the east -- CDU, SPD and PDS.
The PDS, the self-styled champion of an oppressed east, has locked up about 20 percent of the regional vote.

Its successes in the 1994 polls helped shave Kohl's majority in Bonn to a razor-thin lead and force the CDU into three "grand coalitions" with the SPD in eastern states because the reformed communists were considered too compromised to work with.

The SPD agreed in 1994 to form a minority government in Saxony-Anhalt state with Greens coalition partners and tacit support from the PDS. It has worked so well that the SPD is now toying with the idea of left-wing fronts in two other states.

The CDU strategy, now visible after the dramatic defections of the civil rights campaigners in mid-December, is to sap the strength of the parties involved by wooing away their most prestigious eastern members -- the dissidents who defied the communists before and during 1989.

For the past two years, the CDU has moved closer to those activists who feel politically homeless now that the parties they joined move slowly towards a broad left-wing front as their only hope of winning power from the veteran Kohl.
The most prominent defector was Vera Lengsfeld, a Greens deputy whose husband spied on her for the hated Stasi police while she was one of East Germany's few courageous dissidents.
"I campaigned openly against the communist regime from the early 1980s," she said in announcing her switch. "Now I want to help make sure their successors never have power again."
CDU secretary-general Peter Hintze, whose strategy has included two Kohl visits to leading dissident Baerbel Bohley, was triumphant about his pre-Christmas coup.
"With their decision, these representatives of the peaceful revolution against the communist regime show the CDU is the best defender of the ideals of unity in freedom," he crowed.
Most leaders of the Greens and SPD -- one of the defectors was the former Social Democratic deputy Angelika Barbe -- promptly denounced the apostates as traitors.
But some easterners, like former Greens deputy Konrad Weiss, warned the Western-dominated parties not to underestimate the risks involved in cosying up to the PDS.
The SPD sees little alternative to left-wing alliances in the east if it wants to break out of its role as the permanent number two party of German politics.
Although it still rules out a PDS-supported government on the national level, the party recently drafted a position paper that called the PDS one of the forces for reform in the east.
"The SPD in east Germany cannot avoid working with the PDS if this is what the voters want," said the paper drafted by Wolfgang Thierse, the leading eastern Social Democrat in Bonn.
Thierse acknowledged that this strategy played right into the hands of the CDU, which ran a lurid anti-communist campaign in 1994 after the SPD took over Saxony-Anhalt:
"There is no simple way out of this dilemma either. The SPD's strategic goal must be maximum damage limitation."
KOHL READY TO MANOEUVRE

Master tactician Kohl, who all but ignored the east German dissidents for years, seems ready to make the domestic twists and turns needed to ensure he is re-elected to pursue his main goal -- the launch of Europe's single currency.

The chancellor oscillated between labour-friendly stands at the start and end of 1996 and a period of tough pro-business law-making in between. Neither that nor his concessions to the tax-cutting FDP show a clear line for 1997.
But, as Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung commented, the CDU still has the powerful trump card of an active strategy for staying in power compared to the SPD's uncertain manoeuvering.

Kohl's coalition may be divided, as the paper noted, but it at least is determined to stay in power. This gives it a powerful trump card over the uncertain SPD, which seems to be backing into a compromise with the PDS.
"If voters don't trust the SPD to offer real alternatives and change things, then the party with the best strategy wins. Here the CDU is miles ahead of the SPD," the paper wrote.
"It is unlikely that voters will decide at the next election to replace lame rulers with blind ones." REUTER
